title: Verify the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck transition law and equilibrium
statement: For the one-dimensional Itô process dX_t=−a X_t dt+sqrt(2D)dW_t, with a,D>0 and deterministic X_0=x_0, reproduce the Gaussian transition law with mean x_0 exp(−at) and variance (D/a)(1−exp(−2at)). Verify its Fokker–Planck equation, normalization, weak initial limit, Gaussian composition law and stationary density proportional to exp(−a x^2/(2D)). Check zero stationary probability current and detailed balance.
source_locator: Bazant lecture 14, pp.4–5 and Appendix A.1–A.2, pp.7–8; Tong, Section 3.2.2, equations (3.28)–(3.31).
status_basis: The transition and equilibrium formulas are established results in the cited lectures. The verification checklist is a curator-selected calibration task.
plain_summary: Check a standard random process that is pulled toward the origin while experiencing noise. Its exact probability distribution offers a controlled way to verify stochastic equations, stationary distributions and equilibrium claims.
assumptions: W_t is standard one-dimensional Brownian motion and the SDE uses the Itô convention.
a and D are fixed positive real constants; x_0 is deterministic; time is nonnegative and space is the entire real line.
The drift is restoring, −a x, and the noise coefficient is sqrt(2D); there are no boundaries, absorbing states or time-dependent parameters.
Use p_t(y|x) for the transition density from x to y; detailed balance means pi(x)p_t(y|x)=pi(y)p_t(x|y) for the stationary density pi.
scope: The exact scalar Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model with additive Gaussian noise. No interacting-particle model, colored noise, parameter fitting or physical measurement.
target: A matched SDE and density derivation, plus explicit checks of normalization, the weak initial condition, composition, stationarity and detailed balance.
success_criteria: Recover the mean and variance from the integrating-factor representation and the Itô isometry.
Verify ∂_t p=a ∂_y(y p)+D ∂_yy p for t>0, with the same drift and noise normalization as the SDE.
Show normalization, nonnegative density, weak convergence to delta_x at t down to zero and Gaussian kernel composition for positive times.
Normalize the stationary Gaussian with variance D/a, check zero current j(y)=−a y pi(y)−D pi'(y), and verify detailed balance.
Explain that agreement with the mathematical equilibrium distribution does not validate a physical noise model.
known_results: The inspected MIT lecture gives the transition mean and variance through both Fourier methods and a stochastic integrating factor.
The current form of the Fokker–Planck equation connects conservative drift with an equilibrium density under the stated boundary assumptions.
prerequisites: Basic Itô integration, deterministic integrating factors and the Itô isometry.
Fokker–Planck equations, probability current and weak convergence.
significance: A continuous stochastic benchmark with several independent checks. It tests equation translation and equilibrium reasoning that also appear in molecular models, while leaving physical adequacy to separate evidence.

relations.explanation: The harmonic restoring drift provides a reference before checking the equilibrium current for a nonlinear quartic potential. Its explicit transition kernel does not transfer to that nonlinear case.

requirements.experiment: None for the stochastic theorem. A physical Brownian-motion interpretation would require measurements and justification of the noise and overdamped approximations.
requirements.data: No empirical observations. All inputs are symbolic model constants and initial conditions.
requirements.compute: Symbolic differentiation, Gaussian integration and a few exact identities. A local computer algebra environment is a plausible resource class; no simulation campaign, runtime or cost measurement is required or reported.
requirements.theoretical_assumptions: Standard Brownian increments, Itô dynamics, constant positive coefficients and an unbounded state space with Gaussian decay.

ai_assessment.rationale: The closed-form kernel can be checked by both stochastic and differential-equation routes. The main value is whether a generated derivation keeps its conventions and limiting statements consistent.

obstacles: Losing the factor of two in the noise coefficient or using an anti-restoring drift.
Confusing standard deviation with variance in the Gaussian normalization.
Treating a delta initial condition as a pointwise limit of densities.
Inferring physical fluctuation–dissipation relations from arbitrary a and D without a model interpretation.

steps: Derive the stochastic integrating-factor solution and compute its first two moments.
Insert the resulting Gaussian into the forward equation and check normalization analytically.
Prove the weak initial limit against bounded continuous test functions and verify the Gaussian composition identity.
Compute the normalized stationary density, boundary decay and current.
Verify detailed balance by comparing both sides as functions of the two positions and time.
Have a reviewer compare all conventions with the source SDE and its Appendix A.2, rather than relying on imperfect extracted formula text.
validation.human_review_difficulty: Moderate: formulas are explicit, but the probability-space assumptions and weak limit need a reviewer familiar with stochastic processes.
validation.statement_alignment: The verified kernel must belong to the exact SDE written here. Numerical paths or moment agreement alone do not establish the density, semigroup or equilibrium interpretation.

known_attempts: MIT lecture 14 contains the known Fokker–Planck and stochastic-integral derivations; Appendix A.2 credits Geraint Jones.
Tong's kinetic-theory notes develop the probability-current and equilibrium interpretation.
unresolved_checks: Select a symbolic checker and specify which analytic steps remain for human review.
If a physical application is proposed, separately identify mobility, temperature and the evidence supporting the noise model.
